summary: A description of the user-side Telnet program built into UCSB's Online System. It lets a terminal on that system act like an ordinary teletype and log in to other time-sharing hosts across the ARPANET. It covers how to start it, the virtual teletype, how to return to it, and what happens on network errors.

plainLanguage.summary: UCSB's User TELNET let a local terminal act like a teletype connected to a remote computer. It translated typed keys and incoming output so the two systems could work together.

subtitle: How UCSB's User TELNET mapped a local terminal to a remote time-sharing system.

tldr.problem: UCSB Online System terminals differed from teletypes, so users needed a way to reach remote time-sharing systems through the Network.
tldr.mechanism: A User TELNET maps the local keyboard and display to a virtual teletype using a 7-bit ASCII character set, and works with a Server TELNET at the remote site.
tldr.outcome: RFC 206 documents a preliminary implementation, including how users connect, return to TELNET, break connections, and respond to network errors.

sections.title: The User TELNET
sections.content:
RFC 206 describes an initial User TELNET implemented within UCSB's Online System. It lets an Online System user connect to a teletype-compatible time-sharing system at another Network site and use it as if directly connected.

A User TELNET works with a Server TELNET at the remote site. The two programs use the Network Control Programs and a Network-standard connection protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The local program makes the user's terminal look like a teletype to the remote system. The remote program performs the matching conversion at the other end.

sections.title: The Virtual Teletype
sections.content:
The protocol uses a virtual teletype with a 7-bit ASCII character set. The User TELNET maps the UCSB keyboard to those characters and maps remote output to the local storage scope.

For example, UCSB's CASE key acts like a control key for a following letter. Because the storage scope cannot display lowercase letters, the program displays them as uppercase; selected control characters appear in a reserved area at the top of the display.
sections.plainLanguage: The program converts local keys into the virtual teletype's characters. It also changes incoming text to fit the local display.

sections.title: Connecting and Ending a Session
sections.content:
The user starts TELNET, enters a decimal site number, then enters the Server TELNET socket number, normally 1. Once connected, the user logs in according to the remote system's rules and can leave TELNET temporarily and return to the same session.

The user can terminate the Network connection with the documented commands. The RFC warns that ending the connection does not necessarily log the user out of the remote system, and it lists codes for connection, input, and output errors.
sections.plainLanguage: The user selects a remote site and socket, then follows that site's login steps. Leaving the network session may not log the user out of the remote computer.
